//: Corn (field and popcorn) and on-farm grain storage. Every agronomic entry is scoped by deviceNamePattern to a placeholder (%corn% in the field, %bin% for storage) — rename your devices to match, or replace the pattern with deviceProfiles, before trusting any alert. Thresholds are the published extension figures cited in each entry; they are starting points, not calibrations. Popcorn: no popcorn-specific temperature or degree-day tables are published; the UW and Purdue popcorn guides describe growth requirements as similar to dent corn with slower germination and seedling growth, so the dent-corn figures are used throughout.
//months: activeMonths are US Corn Belt timing (planting mid-April to May, silking July, maturity September). Shift them for your latitude and planting date.
//not-yet: GDD staging is corn-gdd-stage below: set its planting date and the hybrid's rating before enabling it.
//enabled: Enabled: checks whose threshold is a published figure the sensor measures directly — air, leaf and soil temperature, humidity, durations, rates, pH. Disabled: checks whose threshold depends on this soil or this probe (volumetric moisture, EC, N, the 'wet' cut-off of a leaf-wetness sensor) or that need the forecast block — each says what to set before enabling it.

checks.//: ═══ FLEET HEALTH — every pack carries these, so the pack runs on its own. None needs crop tuning. ═══

SOIL WARM ENOUGH TO PLANT. Iowa State: plant into soil at or above 10 °C (50 °F) with a forecast that keeps it warming; the first 24–48 h after planting are when imbibitional chilling injures the seed. ISU gives no sustained-days rule, so this raises (info) once soil.temperature has held ≥10 °C unbroken for 24 h — read it together with corn-cold-after-planting-forecast. Source: ISU Integrated Crop Management, "Imbibitional chilling or cold injury", https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/post/imbibitional-chilling-or-cold-injury

COLD SNAP IN THE 48 HOURS AFTER PLANTING. ISU: seed imbibing water in soil in the low 40s °F (~4–7 °C) is injured, and planting 12–36 h ahead of cold, wet weather should be avoided. The forecast carries air, not soil, temperature, so a 4 °C air minimum is a proxy for the soil falling into the injury range. DISABLED: needs the top-level forecast block and a Weatherbit key. Source: ISU, "Imbibitional chilling and frost damage in corn and soybean seedlings" (2014), https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/cropnews/2014/05/imbibitional-chilling-and-frost-damage-corn-and-soybean-seedlings

GDD STAGING by the corn method: 86/50 °F — the day's maximum capped at 86 °F and minimum floored at 50 °F, then (max + min) / 2 − 50 — counted from planting. For a 2700-GDD hybrid Purdue gives silking (R1) near 1400 and black layer (R6) at the hybrid's rating, 2700–3100 across common hybrids; late planting needs fewer ('GDD compression'). DISABLED: set since to this field's planting date (YYYY-MM-DD) and the R6 milestone to the hybrid's rated GDD to black layer. Popcorn has no published GDD table; use the hybrid's rating. Sources: Purdue, "Heat Unit Concepts Related to Corn Development", https://www.agry.purdue.edu/ext/corn/news/timeless/heatunits.html ; UK AGR-202, https://publications.mgcafe.uky.edu/sites/publications.ca.uky.edu/files/agr202.pdf

═══ FROST ═══ Purdue: before about V5 the growing point is below ground, so leaf frost on a seedling is usually survivable; it takes ≤ −2.2 °C (28 °F) for several hours to reach the growing point. In the fall ~0 °C for a few hours kills leaves and −2.2 °C for minutes kills the plant — which is why the spring check is a duration and the fall check is a peak. Sources: Purdue, "Corny Growing Points", https://www.agry.purdue.edu/ext/corn/news/timeless/growingpoints.html ; Purdue, "Frost/freeze injury", https://www.agry.purdue.edu/ext/corn/news/articles.02/frost_freeze-0520.html

Spring: −2.2 °C (28 °F) held for 2 h. Purdue: "Most agronomists agree that 'lethally cold' temperatures for young corn are those that dip to 28°F or lower for 1 to 2 hours"; SDSU: "28° F or colder for 2 hours" is likely damaging if not lethal. The growing point stays below ground until about V5–V6, and cold reaches it more easily in dry, bare soil. A node in air measures the canopy, not the soil; assess stands 3–5 days after. Sources: Purdue (Nielsen), https://extension.entm.purdue.edu/newsletters/pestandcrop/article/assessing-frost-cold-temperature-injury-to-young-corn ; SDSU, https://extension.sdstate.edu/late-spring-frost-damage-corn-and-soybeans
Spring: leaf frost. Survivable before V5; raised so that the stand can be checked 3–5 days later for regrowth from the whorl.
Fall: killing freeze before black layer. −2.2 °C for minutes kills the whole plant; the yield hit depends on how far short of R6 the crop is.

═══ POLLINATION ═══ Iowa State: above 35 °C (95 °F) with low humidity, exposed silks desiccate and pollen viability falls; above 38 °C (100 °F) pollen can be killed outright. ISU is explicit that heat alone does little harm when soil moisture is adequate, so read these with corn-root-zone-dry. No numeric VPD threshold for silking is published, so none is set. Source: ISU, "Corn pollination: effect of high temperature and stress", https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/corn-pollination-effect-high-temperature-and-stress

ROOT ZONE DRY during the drought-sensitive window (V12 through R2). The 15 % floor is the example config's generic volumetric figure — replace it with the value your soil reaches at ~55 % depletion of available water (FAO-56 depletion fraction p for maize is 0.55). Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Table 22, https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e0e.htm

═══ WATERLOGGING ═══ Purdue and ISU: soil oxygen is exhausted about 48 h after saturation. Young corn survives up to ~4 days ponded when it is cool (≤ mid-70s °F), but less than 24 h when it is above 25 °C (77 °F) — hence two entries, the warm one gated on temperature. The 45 % saturation value is a placeholder: set it to the volumetric moisture your probe reads at saturation in this soil. Sources: Purdue, "Effects of ponding on young corn", https://www.agry.purdue.edu/ext/corn/news/timeless/pondingyoungcorn.html ; ISU, "Ponding impacts on corn growth and development", https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/ponding-impacts-corn-growth-development

Warm version: 24 h saturated while the soil is above 25 °C. The gate reads soil.temperature from the same uplink, which the multi-parameter probes carry; ISU's figure is air or water temperature, and soil at seed depth tracks it closely in ponded ground.

NITROGEN — INDICATIVE ONLY. The Iowa State late-spring soil nitrate test (LSNT) threshold is 25 ppm NO3-N in a 0–12 in core taken when corn is 6–12 in tall. An in-situ NPK probe (dragino/lsnpk01, netvox/r72632a01) does not measure the same thing as a lab LSNT on a dried core, so this is DISABLED until the probe has been checked against lab tests on this field. Source: ISU, "Late-spring soil nitrate test (LSNT) use" (2019), https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/cropnews/2019/05/late-spring-soil-nitrate-test-lsnt-use-2019

═══ GRAIN STORAGE ═══ Purdue AED-20: normal grain temperature change is 1–2 °F a week, and any continual rise is the warning sign of insects or mold; keep grain within 15–20 °F of the monthly average air temperature, cool to 1.7–4.4 °C (35–40 °F) for winter, and warm no higher than 10–16 °C (50–60 °F) if storing into summer. K-State: a hot spot can climb from 20 °C to 65 °C and fall again within about two weeks, so it has to be caught while rising. No source gives a numeric "hotter than its neighbours" delta, so none is used. Sources: Purdue AED-20, "Managing Dry Grain in Storage", https://www.extension.purdue.edu/extmedia/aed/aed-20.html ; K-State, "Temperature Monitoring" (Stored Product Protection ch. 23), https://entomology.k-state.edu/doc/finished-chapters/s156-ch-23-temperature-monitoring.pdf
checks.//paths: smartrural/grain-probe-01 reports each cable position as an entry of channels[]. The path channels.0.temperature reads position 0 (Postgres #>> indexes the array), so each position gets its own entry. Single-point probes emit top-level temperature and are the second candidate.

checks.//: Sustained warming: a least-squares slope over two weeks above 1 °C/week (0.006 °C/h). leastSquares with minR2 keeps a one-off aeration swing from counting as a trend.
Summer ceiling: Purdue's 10–16 °C (50–60 °F) is the most grain should be warmed to when held into summer. Raised above 16 °C sustained for a day.

Winter target not reached: Purdue says cool to 1.7–4.4 °C (35–40 °F) for winter storage. Raised (info) if grain is still above 5 °C for a sustained two days in mid-winter — aeration has not caught up.
